title: Saved for ten years to buy a car, but didn't until mom's cancer diagnosis taught me delayed gratification has a prerequisite
dek: He spent a decade saving for a Tesla, repeatedly redirecting funds to real estate and stocks; his mother's pancreatic cancer diagnosis—where a breakthrough targeted drug extends life by only 8 to 9 months—taught him that delayed gratification requires a prerequisite: you must live to enjoy the payoff.
why: Five listeners face spending dilemmas, but Junyan's story hits hardest: ten years of deferred reward crashing into his mother's cancer diagnosis.
who: For anyone wrestling with whether to spend money on themselves, especially those who habitually defer gratification and don't dare celebrate their own wins.

points.h: Major life transitions have no fixed timeline; settling becomes your life
points.body: Ayu bought a transition apartment at 21 with parental help, expecting to leave within a decade. Instead she stayed indefinitely, never replacing inherited furniture and appliances from the previous owner. She slowly realized that major life transitions—marriage, new status—have no predetermined timeline. Days simply accumulate until you recognize you're living permanently in what was supposed to be temporary. That recognition pushed her to finally invest 5,000+ yuan in a new armchair.

points.h: This trip is a gift you're giving yourself, not your parents
points.body: Mumu has wanted to take his parents and younger brother on a trip to Beijing and Shanghai for two or three years but hasn't dared mention it. He's explicit about his motive: this isn't a gift to thank them, it's a gift to himself. He wants them to perform the role of perfect parents in a harmonious family, replacing childhood memories of his parents fighting, throwing dishes, breaking things. He thinks perhaps a faint hint of love exists somewhere in the family; the trip is meant to amplify it.

points.h: He calculated a 70 per cent probability the family would fight about money
points.body: Mumu's worst-case scenario is a public family argument at a tourist site, with his parents accusing him and his brother of wasteful spending and calling relatives to complain. He's assigned this outcome a 70 per cent probability. His father wants the money reserved for his brother's wedding; his mother wants him to fund a rural house renovation that no one will ever occupy. Mumu has already paid for home renovations and his brother's tuition and rent. Yet he hasn't abandoned the idea—just scaled it to a modest New Year trip to nearby cities.

points.h: A single sentence in a college politics class ended six years of score anxiety
points.body: Xiaobai built self-confidence through test scores in middle and high school. In a college politics class, his teacher posed a question that struck him: ‘You worked so hard to get into a 985 university—is it just so you can sell yourself at a better price in the job market?’ The question cracked his score-based self-esteem. He spent years reading heavily to escape what he calls his ‘existential crisis’, and in the process gained new insight into why Apple built such an addictive brand.

points.h: Running short on budget for a bracelet turned into an unexpected gift
points.body: Daisy quit her job at a top-tier hospital and spent three years preparing for the US medical licensing exam. She wanted to buy a Van Cleef & Arpels red five-leaf clover bracelet to mark the end of her days in sterile gloves. But unemployment left her anxious; she hesitated and even researched crystal alternatives. Her laptop broke during the 11.11 sales event, consuming her budget. She met with her graduate advisor to talk through her anxiety—the advisor, knowing nothing of the bracelet, casually gave her an amber bracelet and said: ‘There's no setback in life you can't survive, and nothing you lose that you can't bear.’

points.h: He spends freely on family happiness but treats his own emotional needs as worthless
points.body: Junyan's consumer rule is simple: first decide if something is an investment or a consumption expense. If it's consumption, reject it. That's why the Tesla never happened. But the rule doesn't apply to others. Whenever family members want a new phone, he satisfies the request immediately. He flies economy, uses an iPhone11 Pro. When asked why, he can't explain it. He just believes he cannot measure the emotional value he brings to people around him, so his own emotional value has never felt worth serious consideration.

points.h: Delayed gratification only works if you're sure you'll live to enjoy the payoff
points.body: Junyan wanted to buy a Tesla a decade ago. He invested the money he earned in university into Tesla stock, which grew 8 to 9 times, then moved all of it into Australian real estate. The car was never bought. Two years ago, his mother was diagnosed with mid-stage pancreatic cancer. Only about 20 per cent of pancreatic cancer patients are eligible for surgery. The first breakthrough targeted drug ever discovered for this disease extends life by an average of 8 to 9 months. That diagnosis taught him something new about the principle he'd lived by for years: delayed gratification has a prerequisite. You must first be certain you have a future.

quotes.text: Over these years I gradually realized something: major life transitions don't have a fixed timeline. Days just pass one by one until here you are.
Why should I compromise my current daily quality of life for someone I don't know when or where will appear?
Because I think this trip isn't a gift for them—it's a gift for me. I want them to be my perfect parents, to create a perfect and harmonious family.

Comparing grades, comparing material things—it never ends. There's always someone better than you, always someone outperforming you in the field you chose, always someone with a better starting point. So comparison is stupid and meaningless.

He said that means you haven't experienced enough setbacks. He said actually you'll eventually discover that there's no setback in life you can't get through, and nothing you lose that you can't bear.

I can't measure the emotional value of the people around me. So whenever the people close to me—family members, for instance—say they want the latest phone or something, I satisfy them immediately. But I use an iPhone11 Pro.

Only then did I realize that delayed gratification has a prerequisite: you have to actually live to the day of satisfaction. Whether you still want it by then is secondary. The real prerequisite is whether you'll make it to that day—and nobody knows.
